strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem for embodied AI: generating instance-level, physically interactive tabletop scenes rather than only visually plausible 3D scenes. The focus on dense small-object layouts is well motivated and distinct from room-scale scene generation.

The proposed system is practically compelling as an applied/systems contribution, even though no contribution type is explicitly declared. Recasting it this way makes the main value the end-to-end pipeline and simulator-ready outputs, rather than a single new learning algorithm.

The instance-wise decomposition, canonicalization, differentiable rotation optimization, top-view spatial alignment, and Isaac Sim assembly form a coherent pipeline. The DRO and TSA components are technically sensible and directly target the key failure modes of single-image tabletop reconstruction: wrong rotations, scale ambiguity, floating objects, and collisions.

Quantitative results are consistently favorable across perceptual metrics, GPT-based evaluation, collision statistics, user study ratings, and ablations. The reported collision reduction is especially large compared with the baselines, which supports the claim that explicit pose/scale alignment improves physical plausibility.

The supplementary material improves transparency by providing intermediate outputs, prompt templates, efficiency analysis, and demonstrations of robotic manipulation and object editing. The user study is reasonably large, with randomized ordering and exclusion of very fast responses.
weaknesses: The evaluation evidence is weaker than the strong claims suggest. The 78-sample benchmark is not described in enough detail to judge coverage, difficulty, or possible selection bias, and there is no indication of a released standardized test set or ground-truth 3D layouts.

The method relies heavily on proprietary or black-box components, including ChatGPT, Seedream, and Hunyuan3D-3.0. This raises reproducibility concerns and makes it hard to disentangle the contribution of TabletopGen from the capabilities and failure modes of these external models.

The comparison protocol may favor the proposed pipeline. For text input, MesaTask is only compared qualitatively, while quantitative comparisons use single-image reconstruction baselines. Since TabletopGen converts text to a reference image and then reconstructs from that image, the evaluation does not fully establish superiority over text-to-3D tabletop generation under matched conditions.

Several metrics are imperfect proxies for the stated goals. LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP under best-view selection can obscure incorrect 3D geometry, GPT-4o scoring is subjective and model-dependent, and collision rates alone do not establish dynamic stability, graspability, or usefulness for policy learning.

The ablations show that DRO and TSA help, but the removed components are replaced by direct MLLM prompting, which is a relatively weak baseline. There is no controlled evaluation of rotation, translation, or scale accuracy against ground truth, so the accuracy of the proposed alignment procedure remains indirectly supported.

The TSA stage depends on synthesized top-view images and MLLM commonsense size estimates, both of which can hallucinate under occlusion, unusual objects, transparent objects, nonstandard tables, or cluttered real-world photos. The paper provides little systematic failure analysis for these cases.

Claims about robotic manipulation readiness are supported mainly by qualitative demonstrations on two tasks rather than quantitative manipulation success rates, stability tests, or integration into policy-learning pipelines. This limits the strength of the embodied-AI impact claim.

Some presentation details are underspecified or inconsistent, such as collision metric naming, exact dataset construction, whether all prompts and model versions are fixed, and how physical properties beyond convex decomposition are assigned. These do not invalidate the idea but reduce confidence in reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant applied/systems problem: generating instance-level, simulation-ready tabletop scenes for embodied AI, where object separability, layout plausibility, and collision behavior matter more than photorealistic single-view appearance alone.

The pipeline is coherent at a high level: instance extraction, per-object completion and image-to-3D generation, canonicalization, rotation optimization, top-view-based scale/translation estimation, and Isaac Sim assembly form a plausible engineering recipe for tabletop scene construction.

The authors evaluate multiple aspects of scene quality, including perceptual similarity, language-model judging, collision rates, user study scores, ablations of DRO/TSA, real-image examples, editing examples, and robotic manipulation demonstrations in the supplement.

The proposed DRO and TSA modules address real failure modes in compositional 3D scene generation, especially yaw estimation, scale ambiguity, object placement, and inter-object collisions. The ablation suggests TSA in particular helps reduce scene-level collisions.
weaknesses: I would treat this as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than primarily an algorithmic one. Under that framing, the paper still needs strong reproducibility and convincing end-to-end evidence, but much of the system relies on closed or underspecified foundation models: ChatGPT, Seedream, Hunyuan3D-3.0, GPT-4o evaluation, and GroundedSAM-v2. This makes the claimed automatic framework hard to reproduce, audit, or attribute scientifically.

The technical novelty is limited. Most of the system is a composition of existing models, and the main new pieces are relatively simple: yaw optimization using silhouette/edge/DINO losses and a top-view heuristic using a generated image plus commonsense size priors. These are reasonable engineering choices, but the paper overstates them as a robust solution to single-view 3D spatial recovery.

The evaluation is not sufficiently convincing. The test set has only 78 samples, its construction is vaguely described, and there is no public benchmark, no ground-truth 3D geometry/layout comparison, no statistical uncertainty, and no clear analysis of failure cases. For a systems paper, the evidence should establish reliability across diverse real-world conditions, not mainly curated qualitative examples.

The quantitative protocol is questionable. Selecting the best of 160 rendered views against the input image can obscure geometry and layout errors, and LPIPS/DINO/CLIP against a single reference view do not validate complete 3D structure. The paper acknowledges view bias but still bases key conclusions on this protocol.

The comparison set is weak and somewhat mismatched. The main quantitative baselines are single-image 3D scene reconstruction methods rather than strong tabletop-specific generation or compositional scene assembly systems. MesaTask, arguably the most relevant text-driven tabletop baseline, is only compared qualitatively, which weakens the text-to-scene claims.

The use of GPT-4o as an evaluator is problematic because related MLLMs are also used throughout the method for category analysis, coordinate alignment, size reasoning, stacking order, and prompt expansion. This creates possible evaluator-method coupling, and the paper does not sufficiently validate GPT judgments against objective measurements or blinded expert assessment.

The claimed physical plausibility is under-supported. Collision rate alone does not establish simulation readiness: stability under gravity, contact quality, mass/inertia realism, graspability, articulation, material properties, and downstream robot policy utility are not rigorously evaluated. The robot manipulation demonstrations are anecdotal rather than a systematic benchmark.

The top-view spatial alignment stage depends on synthesizing a top-view image from the reference image, which can hallucinate object sizes, occluded objects, and placements. This is a central source of error, but the paper does not quantify its reliability or compare it with more principled geometry/layout estimation alternatives.

The method can redraw occluded instances using a generative model, which may improve appearance while breaking faithfulness to the input image. The paper claims image alignment and object-count consistency, but there is no rigorous evaluation of hallucinated or incorrectly completed objects.

Important implementation details are missing or insufficient for reproduction: exact prompts and examples are provided, but model versions, API settings, seeds, failure handling, asset post-processing, collision-shape construction, benchmark inputs, and evaluation scripts are not adequately specified in the main paper. The promise to release code helps, but the submitted evidence remains incomplete.

The writing repeatedly makes very strong claims such as “state-of-the-art,” “collision-free,” and “fully automatic” that are not justified by the scale and rigor of the experiments. The actual results look like a useful prototype, but not a mature or scientifically well-validated contribution for ECCV acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: generating instance-level, physically interactive tabletop 3D scenes for embodied AI, where existing room-scale or single-image scene methods often fail on dense small-object layouts.

The proposed TabletopGen pipeline is well motivated and technically coherent. The decomposition into instance extraction/completion, per-instance image-to-3D generation, canonical alignment, DRO rotation recovery, TSA translation/scale estimation, and simulator assembly is a practical contribution for this problem setting.

The DRO and TSA components are the strongest technical contributions. DRO combines silhouette, edge, and DINOv2 appearance losses for rotation recovery, while TSA uses a synthesized top view plus commonsense size priors and an anchor score to address scale/translation ambiguity from a single view.

The empirical results are encouraging. On 78 diverse scenes, TabletopGen improves over ACDC, Gen3DSR, and MIDI across perceptual metrics, GPT-4o scores, and especially collision metrics, with Col O reduced to 0.42% and Col S to 7.69%.
The ablation study supports the main design choices: removing DRO or TSA degrades visual metrics and substantially increases collisions, especially without TSA.
The user study is relatively large for this type of work, with 126 valid questionnaires and randomized method ordering; the reported human preference margin for TabletopGen is very strong.

The supplementary material improves transparency by providing stage-wise outputs, prompts, efficiency analysis, and manipulation demonstrations in Isaac Sim, which strengthens the case that the outputs are more than static renderings.
weaknesses: The system depends heavily on large proprietary or rapidly changing foundation models, including ChatGPT/GPT-4o-style reasoning, Seedream image generation/completion/top-view synthesis, and Hunyuan3D. This raises reproducibility concerns and makes it difficult to isolate what is due to the proposed method versus upstream model capability.

The evaluation lacks ground-truth 3D pose, scale, and geometry accuracy. The main quantitative evidence relies on image similarity, LLM-based judgment, collision checks, and human preference, but does not directly verify metric layout accuracy against annotated 3D tabletop scenes.

The comparison for text-to-scene generation against MesaTask is only qualitative, while the quantitative comparison is mostly against single-image reconstruction methods. This is understandable given input differences, but it weakens the breadth of the state-of-the-art claim across both text and image settings.

The use of GPT-4o for evaluation is a concern because the method itself also uses MLLM reasoning. The paper should better guard against evaluator bias and report whether prompts, images, and method identities were controlled to avoid favoring the proposed pipeline.

The claimed collision-free/physically plausible generation is somewhat overstated: the method still reports 7.69% scene-level collisions, and physical plausibility is mostly assessed through collision rates and limited Isaac Sim demonstrations rather than extensive stability or manipulation-policy evaluations.

TSA relies on a generated top-view image and commonsense size estimates, both of which can hallucinate or distort spatial relations under occlusion. The paper would benefit from more failure cases and sensitivity analyses for top-view synthesis errors, anchor selection, and size-prior mistakes.

The test set is relatively small and apparently newly constructed, with unclear public availability and limited discussion of sampling protocol. A public benchmark or more standardized evaluation would make the contribution more convincing.

The method is computationally expensive, taking about 32 minutes for a 9-object scene on an RTX 4090, and many stages are sequential. This is acceptable for data generation but limits interactive use and should temper some application claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: generating simulation-ready, instance-interactive tabletop scenes for robotic manipulation data synthesis, rather than only visually plausible 3D scenes. This is a valuable applied/systems contribution even though no contribution type is declared; assessing it as such makes the integrated pipeline and downstream utility more central than algorithmic novelty alone.

The system decomposition is sensible and well motivated. Separating instance extraction, Z-up canonicalization, rotation optimization via DRO, top-view spatial alignment via TSA, and Isaac Sim assembly directly targets common failure modes of single-image 3D scene generation such as fused meshes, floating objects, and interpenetration.

The experiments are broader than many scene-generation papers: image-driven baselines, text-driven baselines, user study, ablations, additional recent-method comparisons, physical collision/stability metrics, and a real-to-sim-to-real manipulation demonstration are all included.

Quantitative results are strong on the reported metrics. The improvements in DINOv2/CLIP, GPT-4o ratings, collision rates, support stability, and user preference suggest that the pipeline produces scenes that are more usable for simulation than the compared baselines.

The paper is generally clear, with useful implementation details, prompts, intermediate outputs, and ablations that isolate the contribution of DRO and TSA. The limitations section is brief but acknowledges the current focus on typical tabletop settings.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a major concern. Core components depend on proprietary or rapidly changing models and services, including ChatGPT, Seedream, and Hunyuan3D-3.0. The paper provides prompts, but not enough to ensure that others can reproduce the same images, instance completions, top views, commonsense sizes, or MLLM judgments.

The evaluation relies heavily on generated images and automated GPT-4o evaluation. Only 4 of the 78 image-driven test scenes are real-world photographs, and the text-to-scene evaluation is mostly GPT-scored. This weakens the evidence for robust real-world generalization and may overstate visual/semantic quality.

The claimed downstream robotic utility is promising but narrow. The real-to-sim-to-real policy experiment uses one reconstructed real tabletop setting, three pick-and-place/stacking tasks, one robot setup, and no comparison against data generated by baselines or against real-data fine-tuning. It supports feasibility, but not the broad claim that TabletopGen is a reliable large-scale data engine for policy learning.

Several technical choices are under-validated. TSA depends on a synthesized top-view image, MLLM-inferred stacking relations, and commonsense object sizes; errors in any of these could systematically distort scale or placement. The paper does not provide enough failure analysis, uncertainty handling, or evaluation under occlusion-heavy, transparent/specular, articulated, deformable, or highly cluttered scenes.

The algorithmic novelty is moderate. DRO combines standard differentiable rendering losses, and TSA is a pragmatic alignment heuristic using top-view synthesis and anchor scaling. The main contribution is an effective system integration, but some claims of state-of-the-art scene quality and physical validity feel stronger than the evidence justifies.

Physical realism is evaluated mostly through collisions and settling/support stability. Important properties for manipulation, such as accurate mass, friction, contact geometry quality, grasp affordances, and task success across diverse generated scenes, are not deeply assessed. Near-zero collision rates alone do not guarantee physically faithful simulation.

Baseline fairness is somewhat hard to judge. Some baselines are not designed for tabletop manipulation or simulation readiness, and the text-driven comparison adapts Holodeck to a tabletop setting. More comparisons to digital-twin or robot-data-generation systems, and stronger baseline tuning details, would make the empirical case more convincing.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: creating simulation-ready tabletop scenes for robotic manipulation, where visual fidelity alone is insufficient and instance-level interactivity, collision geometry, and physical plausibility matter.

The proposed pipeline is coherent at a system level. Decomposing the task into instance extraction, canonical 3D asset generation, rotation optimization, top-view spatial alignment, and Isaac Sim assembly is a reasonable design for tabletop manipulation data synthesis.

The DRO and TSA components are intuitive and practically motivated. The ablations suggest that rotation optimization and top-view/stacking priors both contribute to lower collision rates and better visual alignment.

The paper evaluates more than one aspect of scene quality, including perceptual metrics, collision metrics, GPT-based ratings, a human user study, additional physical stability metrics, and a small real-robot transfer demonstration.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited relative to the breadth of the claims. Much of the system depends on chaining existing black-box models: ChatGPT for reasoning, Seedream for image generation/completion/top-view synthesis, GroundedSAM-v2 for segmentation, Hunyuan3D for assets, PyTorch3D for rendering, Isaac Sim and cuRobo for simulation/planning. The paper’s own algorithmic contribution is mainly pose/scale alignment, which is useful but not enough to fully support the broad 'data engine' and 'state-of-the-art' claims.

Reproducibility is a major concern. Several central components are proprietary or version-sensitive, and the paper does not provide enough detail to reproduce prompts, model settings, failure handling, mesh processing, physical parameters, collision decomposition, or automatic task generation reliably. The results may depend heavily on unavailable commercial models rather than the proposed method.

The evaluation set is small and weak for the claimed generality: 78 scenes total, only 4 real-world photographs, and 30 text-to-scene cases. Most evidence comes from synthesized reference images, which may not reflect real clutter, occlusion, lighting, transparent/specular objects, deformables, articulated objects, or difficult camera viewpoints.

The comparisons may not be fully fair or diagnostic. The method uses powerful current generative models and multiple image/MLLM calls, while baselines are not clearly adapted with comparable external priors or post-processing. For text-to-scene, TabletopGen converts text into a generated reference image, making the task different from direct text-conditioned layout generation baselines.

The reliance on GPT-4o evaluation and unpaid user studies is not enough to establish physical or semantic correctness. GPT-based visual ratings can be biased by image realism, and the user study reports aggregate preferences but lacks statistical tests, participant expertise breakdown, inter-rater agreement, or safeguards against recognizing method-specific artifacts.

The physical plausibility evidence is narrower than claimed. Collision rates, support stability, and 5-second settling are useful but do not establish robust manipulation-readiness. Contact parameters, friction, mass, inertial properties, and gripper-object interactions are not validated in detail, and many generated meshes from image-to-3D models may have poor geometry for real manipulation.

The real-to-sim-to-real validation is promising but too limited to substantiate the broad downstream policy-learning claims. It appears to use one reconstructed real tabletop, three tasks, and 2,000 synthetic trajectories per task, with no comparison against alternative data generation pipelines, no multiple-scene generalization, and substantial sim-to-real gaps on the harder task.

The method depends on hallucinated top-view images and commonsense object sizes from an MLLM, but the paper does not analyze when these hallucinations are wrong. This is especially concerning because TSA’s scale and translation estimates are built directly from generated top-view boxes rather than measured geometry.

The limitations section is very thin. It does not seriously discuss failure modes such as severe occlusion, transparent/reflective objects, thin objects, containers, articulated objects, deformables, dense stacking, incorrect segmentation, wrong canonicalization, hallucinated object categories, or physically incorrect generated meshes.

The writing repeatedly overclaims, using phrases such as 'fully automatic', 'state-of-the-art', 'infinitely' diverse expansion, and 'reliable data engine' without evidence commensurate with those claims. The paper would be stronger if it framed the work as a promising system prototype rather than a broadly validated solution.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and useful Applied/Systems contribution for vision-based 3D tabletop scene generation and robotic manipulation data synthesis. The emphasis on simulation-ready, instance-level interactive scenes addresses a real gap in current single-image/text-to-3D scene generation methods.

The system design is coherent: generative instance extraction, Z-up canonicalization, differentiable rotation optimization, top-view spatial alignment, and Isaac Sim assembly form a plausible end-to-end pipeline. The DRO and TSA components are well motivated for tabletop scenes, where object orientation, support relations, metric scale, and collision-free placement are central.

The experimental evidence is fairly broad for a systems paper. The authors compare against image-driven methods such as ACDC, Gen3DSR, and MIDI, text-driven methods such as MesaTask and Holodeck-table, and additional recent methods in the supplement. Reported gains are consistent across perceptual metrics, GPT-based evaluation, user study ratings, and collision/stability metrics.

The physical-usability evaluation is a notable strength. Collision rates, support stability, dynamic settling stability, qualitative simulator interaction, in-scene editing, and zero-shot real-to-sim-to-real manipulation experiments make the paper more convincing than a purely visual 3D generation benchmark.

The paper is generally clear, with useful implementation details, ablations of DRO and TSA, test-set construction details, camera sweep protocol, user-study description, and prompt templates in the supplement. The qualitative figures also communicate the practical value of instance-level editable scenes.
weaknesses: The main contribution is an effective integration of existing generative and reasoning models rather than a fundamentally new generative model. DRO and TSA add useful tabletop-specific structure, but much of the pipeline depends on ChatGPT, Seedream, Hunyuan3D, GroundedSAM-v2, and Isaac Sim, so the originality is strongest at the system level rather than at the algorithmic level.

Reproducibility is a significant concern. Several key components are proprietary or rapidly changing foundation models, and the paper does not clearly state whether code, prompts, generated test inputs, intermediate annotations, meshes, or exact evaluation scripts will be released. This could make independent verification difficult.

The evaluation set is relatively small and mostly synthetic: 78 image-driven scenes include only 4 real-world photographs, and the text-to-scene comparison uses 30 prompts. Given the strong claims about real-world utility and robustness, more real tabletop images and more diverse failure cases would strengthen the evidence.

Some evaluation signals are potentially biased or weakly controlled. GPT-4o is used both as a pipeline component and as an evaluator, and human preference heavily favors the proposed method but details such as participant expertise and statistical significance are limited. Comparisons also involve methods with different assumptions and capabilities, making attribution of the gains less clean.

The sim-to-real validation is promising but still limited. It appears to use a small number of tasks and scenes, and there is no direct comparison to policies trained with alternative scene-generation/data-synthesis pipelines. Thus, the downstream robotics claim is plausible but not yet fully established.

The paper under-discusses computational cost, latency, failure modes, and sensitivity to upstream model errors. A training-free pipeline built from multiple large generative/MLLM calls may be expensive or brittle in practice, especially for dense scenes, severe occlusion, transparent or reflective objects, articulated objects, and non-tabletop support structures.
